Usury and Lending
YOO-zhuh-ree and LEND-ing
noun phrase (Christian ethics)
The biblical doctrine governing lending and the charging of interest. The OT forbade charging interest (Hebrew neshek, usury) to fellow Israelites in their poverty (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20) while permitting it to foreigners. The historic Christian and Reformed discussion distinguishes oppressive usury (forbidden) from legitimate interest on productive commercial loans (permitted by the Reformers).

📖 Biblical Definition

The biblical doctrine governing lending and the charging of interest. The OT law forbade charging neshek (usury / interest) to fellow Israelites in their poverty: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury (Exodus 22:25; cf. Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20, which forbids usury to a brother but permits it to a foreigner). The substantive concern of the OT law is the protection of the poor brother from exploitation in his distress; the lender is to help the poor brother freely, not to profit from his poverty. The historic Christian discussion developed substantially. The medieval Catholic church prohibited all interest-charging (treating all interest as usury), grounding the prohibition in Aristotle's argument that money is sterile and cannot lawfully breed. The Reformers (especially Calvin) made a substantive distinction: oppressive usury (charging interest to the poor in their distress, exploiting their need) remains forbidden; but legitimate interest on productive commercial loans (where the borrower uses the loan to generate profit and the lender shares in the productive return) is permissible, since the OT prohibition was specifically about the poor brother's distress, not about all interest-charging whatsoever. Calvin's substantive treatment (his letter on usury and his commentaries) distinguishes the exploitative lending the OT forbids from the legitimate commercial lending of a developed economy. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed distinction: the exploitation of the poor through predatory lending (the payday-loan industry, predatory credit-card and consumer-debt practices, the broader debt-slavery of the modern financial system) is forbidden as oppressive usury; legitimate interest on productive commercial loans is permissible; the substantive biblical concern is the protection of the poor and the brother from exploitation, the warning against the bondage of debt (Proverbs 22:7, the borrower is servant to the lender), and the commendation of generous free lending to the poor brother (Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Luke 6:35).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Biblical doctrine governing lending and interest; OT forbade usury to the poor brother (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20); medieval Catholic church prohibited all interest; the Reformers (Calvin) distinguished oppressive usury (forbidden) from legitimate commercial interest (permitted).

USURY AND LENDING, n. phr. (Christian ethics) The doctrine governing lending and interest. OT forbade neshek (usury/interest) to the poor brother (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20, forbidden to a brother but permitted to a foreigner). Substantive concern: protection of the poor brother from exploitation in distress. Medieval Catholic church prohibited all interest (Aristotle's argument that money is sterile). The Reformers (Calvin) distinguished: oppressive usury (charging interest to the poor in distress) forbidden; legitimate interest on productive commercial loans permitted. Patriarchal-Reformed position: predatory lending (payday loans, predatory consumer debt) forbidden as oppressive usury; legitimate commercial interest permitted; the borrower is servant to the lender (Proverbs 22:7).

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 22:25 — "If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury."

Deuteronomy 23:19-20 — "Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother; usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of any thing that is lent upon usury: Unto a stranger thou mayest lend upon usury; but unto thy brother thou shalt not lend upon usury."

Proverbs 22:7 — "The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender."

Luke 6:35 — "But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The biblical doctrine forbids oppressive usury (the exploitation of the poor through predatory lending) while permitting legitimate interest on productive commercial loans (the Reformed distinction); the contemporary predatory-lending and debt-slavery system is the modern oppressive usury.

The biblical doctrine of lending requires the substantive Reformed distinction between oppressive usury (forbidden) and legitimate commercial interest (permitted). The OT law forbade charging interest to the poor brother in his distress (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37), protecting the poor from exploitation. The medieval Catholic church over-extended the prohibition to all interest-charging whatsoever (grounding it in Aristotle's argument that money is sterile and cannot lawfully breed); the Reformers (especially Calvin) corrected this, distinguishing the exploitative lending the OT forbids from the legitimate commercial lending of a developed economy in which the borrower uses the loan productively and the lender shares in the return. The patriarchal-Reformed reader applies the substantive distinction to the contemporary financial order. The modern predatory-lending system — the payday-loan industry charging hundreds of percent annual interest to the desperate poor; the predatory credit-card and consumer-debt practices that ensnare the financially-vulnerable in compounding debt; the broader debt-slavery of a financialized economy — is the modern oppressive usury, forbidden by the substantive biblical concern for the protection of the poor. The patriarchal-Reformed reader also holds the substantive biblical warning against the bondage of debt (Proverbs 22:7, the borrower is servant to the lender) and the commendation of generous free lending to the poor brother (Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Luke 6:35); the household-economy vision counsels substantive freedom from consumer debt and substantive generosity toward the poor brother.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

OT prohibition of usury to the poor brother (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19-20); medieval Catholic total prohibition; Calvin's distinction of oppressive usury from legitimate commercial interest.
